items.new: But it so happened just then that it was high time for the Captain to mind his own eye. The tremendous strain on the mainsail had snapped the weather-sheet, and the huge boom was now flying from side to side, sweeping the entire after part of the deck. The poor fellow Queequeg had handled so roughly was swept overboard; all hands were in a panic; and to try snatching at the boom to stop it seemed madness. It flew from right to left and back again almost in one tick of a watch, and every instant seemed about to snap into splinters. Nothing was done, and nothing seemed possible to do; those on deck rushed toward the bows and stood eyeing the boom as if it were the lower jaw of an enraged whale. In the midst of this consternation, Queequeg dropped deftly to his knees, and crawling under the path of the boom, whipped hold of a rope, made one end fast to the bulwarks, and then, flinging the other like a lasso, caught it around the boom as it swept over his head; at the next jerk the spar was trapped that way, and all was safe. The schooner was brought up into the wind, and while the hands were clearing away the stern boat, Queequeg, stripped to the waist, darted from the side in a long, living arc of a leap. For three minutes or more he was seen swimming like a dog, throwing his long arms straight out in front of him, and by turns showing his brawny shoulders through the freezing foam. I looked at the grand and glorious fellow, but saw no one to be saved. The greenhorn had gone down. Shooting himself straight up out of the water, Queequeg now took an instant's glance around him, and seeming to see just how matters stood, dived down and disappeared. A few minutes more, and he rose again, one arm still striking out, and with the other dragging a lifeless form. The boat soon picked them up. The poor bumpkin was revived. All hands voted Queequeg a noble trump; the captain begged his pardon. From that hour I clung to Queequeg like a barnacle — yes, until poor Queequeg took his last long dive.

items.new: And so these naked Nantucketers, these sea hermits, issuing from their anthill in the sea, have overrun and conquered the watery world like so many Alexanders, parceling out the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans among themselves, as the three pirate powers did Poland. Let America add Mexico to Texas, and pile Cuba on top of Canada; let the English overswarm all India, and hang out their blazing banner from the sun; two thirds of this globe of land and water belong to the Nantucketer. For the sea is his; he owns it, as Emperors own empires, other seamen having only a right of way through it. Merchant ships are only extension bridges; armed ones only floating forts; even pirates and privateers, though they follow the sea as highwaymen follow the road, only plunder other ships, other fragments of the land like themselves, without seeking to draw their living from the bottomless deep itself. The Nantucketer — he alone resides and riots on the sea; he alone, in Bible language, goes down to it in ships, plowing it to and fro as his own special plantation. There is his home; there lies his business, which a Noah's flood would not interrupt, though it overwhelmed all the millions in China. He lives on the sea as prairie cocks do on the prairie; he hides among the waves, he climbs them as chamois hunters climb the Alps. For years he does not know the land; so that when he comes to it at last, it smells like another world, stranger than the moon would to an Earthman. Like the landless gull, which at sunset folds her wings and is rocked to sleep between the billows, so at nightfall the Nantucketer, out of sight of land, furls his sails and lays himself down to rest, while under his very pillow rush herds of walruses and whales.

items.new: It was quite late in the evening when the little Moss came snugly to anchor and Queequeg and I went ashore; so we could attend to no business that day, at least none but a supper and a bed. The landlord of the Spouter-Inn had recommended us to his cousin Hosea Hussey of the Try Pots, who, he claimed, ran one of the best-kept hotels in all Nantucket; and he had also assured us that Cousin Hosea, as he called him, was famous for his chowders. In short, he plainly hinted that we could not possibly do better than try potluck at the Try Pots. But the directions he had given us — keep a yellow warehouse on our starboard hand till we came in sight of a white church to port, then keep that on the port hand till we made a corner three points to starboard, and that done, ask the first man we met where the place was — these crooked directions of his puzzled us very much at first, especially as, right at the start, Queequeg insisted that the yellow warehouse, our first point of departure, must be left on the port hand, whereas I had understood Peter Coffin to say it was on the starboard. However, by beating about a little in the dark, and now and then knocking up a peaceable inhabitant to ask the way, we at last came to something there was no mistaking.

The horns of the cross-trees had been sawed off on the other side, so that this old topmast looked not a little like a gallows. Perhaps I was oversensitive to such impressions at the time, but I could not help staring at this gallows with a vague misgiving. I got a sort of crick in my neck as I gazed up at the two remaining horns — yes, two of them, one for Queequeg and one for me. It's ominous, I think. A Coffin for my innkeeper on landing in my first whaling port; tombstones staring at me in the whalemen's chapel; and here a gallows! And a pair of prodigious black pots too! Are these last throwing out sly hints about Tophet, that biblical place of fire?
